tasks.title: Package skeleton, command-line stub, requirements.txt
tasks.why_tier: One obvious right answer: names, signatures and error codes are all given in spec section 2.
tasks.brief: Create the package folder `mlprofessor` (spec 2). `mlprofessor.profile` with exactly the signature and defaults of 2.1; for now it may raise NotImplementedError. A `ProfileResult` class (2.3) to be filled later. `mlprofessor/errors.py` with every class of 2.4, each subclassing `ProfileError` and carrying its `code`. `mlprofessor/extensions.py` with the context manager `use(families=None, steps=None)` exactly as 2.6 describes (it stores the overrides, restores the previous state on exit including after an exception, and nests). An empty module `mlprofessor/stages.py` that later tasks fill. The command line of 2.2: `python -m mlprofessor profile` with every option, calling `profile`, exit codes 0, 2 and 3; `--help` must exit 0. `requirements.txt` pinning pandas==3.1.1, numpy==2.5.4, scikit-learn==1.9.1 and threadpoolctl==3.8.0. Install nothing: all four are already in the interpreter, and the package itself is never installed.

tasks.title: Load one table; count usable rows
tasks.why_tier: Carries F6: a row lost here is lost from every count that follows.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.load_table(data)` and `stages.usable_rows(frame, target, time_col=None)` (spec 2.7), implementing step 1 and step 2 of section 3 and the loading rules of section 6. Read spec section 9 first: pandas 3 renames duplicate headers silently, skips blank lines, and turns the first column into an index when rows are longer than the header. The loader reads the header line itself to catch duplicates. `row` positions are fixed here and never change.

tasks.title: Column roles that need no target
tasks.why_tier: Carries F6 and decides which columns ever reach a model.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.column_roles(frame, target, time_col=None)` (spec 2.7): the rule table of step 5, in its order, with the cut-offs of 4.3 and the date forms of 4.5. Roles are judged on the usable rows; `n_missing`, `n_coerced` and `n_infinite` are counted over every row. Whole numbers are judged by value, never by dtype (a blank cell makes an integer column float). Never use pandas' date parser to decide whether a column is a date. A number written with thousands separators (`1,200`; the pattern is pinned in step 5) is never parsed, and a column is never used with such cells left out. Rule 4a comes before the coercion rule: a column in which at least 90% of the non-missing values parse or match the pattern, and at least one matches, is excluded with the reason `numeric_with_separators`, whether it is written that way throughout or is plain numbers with a single such cell (D28, D34). A column whose text cells are of another kind (`abc`) is still read as numeric with those cells coerced, and one holding `1,200` in every row is `constant`. This function returns no warnings.

tasks.title: Task decision
tasks.why_tier: Carries F5: the wrong task puts the headline on the wrong scale.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.decide_task(values, task="auto")` (spec 2.7, step 4 of section 3). Count distinct values; ignore the type for the two-value rule. Raise the named errors rather than guess. Return the classes in sorted order with the second as the positive class, and the `whole_number_regression_target` warning code when the rule picks regression on whole numbers.

tasks.title: Random holdout and folds
tasks.why_tier: Decides which rows every number is computed on.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.split_random(n_rows, classes=None, seed=0)` (spec 2.7, step 7 of section 3, random scheme): the holdout of ceil(n/4) rows first, stratified when `classes` is given, then five folds that partition the remaining rows. Everything comes from the seed.

tasks.title: Time column, time-ordered holdout, expanding folds, gap
tasks.why_tier: Carries F7: a training row at or after the holdout, or a misread date, gives an optimistic number with no error.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.read_time(values)` and `stages.split_time(keys, gap=0)` (spec 2.7; steps 3 and 7 of section 3). `read_time` accepts exactly the three forms of step 3 and raises `TimeColumnError` for anything else; text is matched against the ISO 8601 pattern before any parsing, and day-first or month-first text is never parsed. `split_time` cuts at whole timestamps, makes six contiguous blocks as numpy.array_split would, and takes the gap off before the holdout and before every validation block.

tasks.title: Metrics, skill and the previous-value baseline
tasks.why_tier: Carries F4 and F8; exact arithmetic that every headline rests on.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.roc_auc`, `stages.mse`, `stages.skill` and `stages.previous_value` (spec 2.7; step 11 of section 3). ROC AUC by ranks with ties sharing their average rank, in numpy. Accuracy is not a metric here.

tasks.title: Preprocessing fitted on the rows it is given
tasks.why_tier: Carries F1: preprocessing that learns from the wrong rows is the small, invisible form of leakage.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.Preprocessor(kinds)` with `fit(frame)` and `transform(frame)` (spec 2.7; 'Preprocessing' under step 8 of section 3): median imputation and standardisation for numeric columns, the level `(missing)` and one-hot columns for at most the 30 most frequent levels for categorical columns. Every statistic comes from the frame given to `fit`.

tasks.title: Fit, select, score once: the run in memory, random scheme, fast profile
tasks.why_tier: Carries F1 and F3: this is where a refit on the wrong rows or a cross-validation score as the headline would happen.
tasks.brief: Make `profile()` run in memory under the random scheme with `profile="fast"`, following steps 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10 and 11 of spec section 3 by calling the step functions already built: load, usable rows, task, roles, the fast profile's random row cap, `split_random`, then for each configuration and fold a fresh `Preprocessor` and model fitted on the fold's training rows, selection by `cv_mean`, one refit on all training rows, one scoring of the holdout, the baselines and skill. The two families of the fast profile are `linear-0` and `tree-0` (4.1). Honour `extensions.use` (2.6): families replace the built-in ones, steps run first, every fit gets fresh objects and DataFrames indexed by source row position. A configuration that raises is recorded as failed and never chosen; all failing raises. Hold BLAS to one thread and OpenMP to `n_jobs` with threadpoolctl for the whole run. Return a `ProfileResult` whose `predictions`, `models`, `rows`, `columns`, `warnings` and `headline` (metric, score, model, baseline, baseline_score, skill) are populated. No time column, no leak screen, no interval, no files yet.

tasks.title: profile.json, predictions.csv and the command line: the first run the gate can judge
tasks.why_tier: First task the gate judges; owns reconciliation between the source, the files and the result object.
tasks.brief: Complete the output of spec section 5 for the random scheme under the fast profile: every key of `profile.json` (5.2), with fields that later tasks fill written as null or empty (the interval and p-value fields, `limitations`); `predictions.csv` (5.1); `to_dict()`, `to_json(path)` and `out_dir`; the DataFrames equal to their JSON parts (2.3). The command line writes both files, prints a short summary, exits 3 with `error: <code>: <message>` on a named error and writes nothing then. Add the warnings that arise in steps 1 to 11: `values_coerced`, `numeric_with_separators` (one per column excluded with that reason by rule 4a of step 5; it has no other form), `infinite_values`, `blank_header`, `duplicate_rows`, `whole_number_regression_target`, `small_holdout`, `fold_not_scored`, `model_failed`. No NaN in the JSON. Only `meta.timing` may hold a clock value.

tasks.title: Time-ordered scheme wired into the run, with its baselines
tasks.why_tier: Carries F7 and F8.
tasks.brief: When `time_col` is given, follow the time-ordered path of spec section 3: read the time column (step 3), drop and count rows with no time value, apply the fast profile's cap as the most recent whole timestamps (step 6, `FastProfileError` for a wide panel), split with `split_time` (step 7), count `dropped_gap` and each fold's `gap_rows`, fill the time fields of `validation` (5.2). Regression baselines under time order (step 11): with unique timestamps score both `training_mean` and `previous_value` and use the lower error; with repeated timestamps use the training mean and raise `autocorrelated_panel_target` above 0.5. When `time_col` is not given and a column was excluded as `datetime`, raise `date_column_undeclared`. `--gap` without `--time-col` is an input error.

tasks.title: Leak screen
tasks.why_tier: Carries F2, and a screen fitted on the wrong rows is itself F1.
tasks.brief: Add the leak screen of step 8 of spec section 3, run on training rows only, before any model: the missing-by-class rule, then the single-column cross-validated skill with the pinned tree over the selection folds, cut-offs of 4.3. Under time order it uses the expanding folds and, for regression with unique timestamps, the previous-value baseline, so a lagged target on a random walk is not flagged. A flagged column is excluded with reason `suspected_leak`, its `leak_rule` and a warning, and reaches no model. The same skill, measured once per column, also decides the warning tier (rule 3 of step 8, D30): at least 0.90 and below 0.98, the column stays a feature and a `strong_single_column` warning names it. No feature left raises `NoFeaturesError`.

tasks.title: Interval and p-value, row and block forms
tasks.why_tier: Decides how certain the headline looks; the resampling must respect time order.
tasks.brief: Add step 12 of spec section 3, from the holdout predictions alone, nothing refitted: the percentile bootstrap interval on score and skill and the permutation p-value under the random scheme; the moving-block bootstrap over distinct holdout timestamps under time order, with the p-value absent and its reason given; no interval below 30 holdout timestamps, with a reason and the `no_interval` warning. Whenever the interval does come from the block bootstrap, add exactly one `interval_approximate` warning with a null column (D27); never under the random scheme. 200 resamples under fast, 1,000 under full. Fill the interval and p-value fields of `headline` (5.2).

tasks.title: Random forest and histogram gradient boosting behind the existing family interface
tasks.why_tier: One concern behind an interface that already exists; the estimators and their arguments are given in spec 4.1.
tasks.brief: Under `profile="full"` run three families in the order linear, forest, boosting (spec 4.1), each with at least its index-0 configuration, for both tasks, through the same family interface the fast profile uses. Forests are fitted with `n_jobs` and predict on one thread. The regression forest's default `max_features` is one third. Keep the handling of a configuration that raises: status `failed`, error text, `model_failed` warning, never chosen; every configuration failing raises `AllModelsFailedError`.

tasks.title: The full profile's grids, and the same result at any n_jobs
tasks.why_tier: Carries F3: with 18 configurations the best cross-validation score is optimistic, and selection must not touch the holdout.
tasks.brief: Complete the grids of spec 4.1: exactly 18 configurations under `full`, named and ordered as given, `params` holding the grid arguments. Selection over all of them by `cv_mean` with ties to the earlier family then the earlier grid position; only the chosen one is refitted and scored on the holdout. `meta.n_jobs` records the cores used. The same seed must give identical files at any `n_jobs` (D17): BLAS on one thread always, OpenMP on `n_jobs`, forests predicting on one thread.

tasks.title: Edges, limitations statement, console summary
tasks.why_tier: A clear contract: every edge, code and fixed text is listed in the spec.
tasks.brief: Walk the table of spec section 7 row by row and make each edge give its named error or its reported outcome; none may be skipped silently. Every invalid argument of 2.1 raises `InputError`. Write the fixed limitations statement (nine strings) and the random-split caveat of 5.4 exactly. Make the console summary short and plain: task, scheme, row counts, skill with its metric, baseline and interval, the p-value when there is one, and each warning.

tasks.title: README with run instructions
tasks.why_tier: Prose from known facts.
tasks.brief: Write `README.md` for a data scientist: what the tool measures and what it does not (the limitations of spec 5.4, in plain words), how to call `mlprofessor.profile` and the command line with the interpreter at E:\CODE\ml-professor\mlprof_env\Scripts\python.exe from the repo root, what `profile.json` and `predictions.csv` contain, the two validation schemes and when to pass `time_col`, the fast profile. tasks.title: Guards for the first review's test holes, and two CSV edges: no code change expected
tasks.why_tier: Nothing is built here. But if a guard fails, the fix is in the code that decides which rows a fitted step sees, the most delicate code in the package.
tasks.brief: NO CODE CHANGE IS EXPECTED. These four test files guard behaviour the application already has: every test in them was measured to pass against the application on 2026-11-17, before this task existed (plan/test-plan.md, 'Second pass'). Run them first. If they all pass, change nothing and finish. If one fails, THE APPLICATION IS WRONG, NOT THE TEST: the tests are locked, and each guard was proved by running it against a copy of the reference implementation that carries exactly the fault it is named for (spec 8.1), or against the reference as it was before the decision the test holds (D42). Fix only what the failing test names, and say in your final message what you found. What each file guards: `test_guard_final_fit.py`, that the statistics of the final fit's imputation and scaling come from training rows only (M1), that one-hot levels come from the rows of each fit only (M2), and that a categorical level is the cell's text without the white space round it, in counting, in the leak screen, in what a step receives and in the matrix (D42; spec step 5); `test_guard_leak_screen.py`, that the leak screen's trees are fitted on each fold's training rows only and its missing-by-class rule counts training rows only (M3); `test_guard_uncertainty.py`, that the block bootstrap draws whole blocks of consecutive timestamps (M4) and that a shuffle whose skill equals the observed skill counts in the p-value (M5); `test_csv_edges.py`, that a file which is not valid UTF-8 is an `input_error` wherever the bad byte sits, that leading lines of only spaces and tabs are skipped when the header is read, as pandas skips them, and that a header cell holding only white space is a name like any other, so that two alike stop the run with `duplicate_columns` (D42; spec 6). These tests join the checks every later task must keep green.

tasks.title: Skill when a baseline's error is zero
tasks.why_tier: Decides which resamples the interval on skill is computed from, and what the headline reports where it has no value.
tasks.brief: When a baseline's squared error on the rows being scored is exactly zero, skill = 1 - error / baseline error has no value, and today the run dies with a ZeroDivisionError and writes nothing (D36). Make it report instead, everywhere skill is computed. (1) The headline, spec step 11: `headline.skill` is null, never an error, an infinity or a zero in its place; exactly one `skill_undefined` warning with a null column says why; the score, every baseline with its score (the zero included) and the rest of the output are reported as usual. (2) The interval, spec step 12: a resample whose baseline error is zero keeps its place in the interval on the score and is left out of the interval on skill only. Count the resamples kept for skill in a new key, `headline.n_resamples_skill_used`; `n_resamples_used` goes on counting those in which the score could be computed. If fewer than half of the resamples can be used for skill, `skill_low` and `skill_high` are null while the interval on the score stands (D40). That is always so when `headline.skill` is null, and the `skill_undefined` warning of (1) covers it: add no other. When `headline.skill` is a number and its interval cannot be computed, add exactly one warning with the code `no_skill_interval` and a null column, and no `skill_undefined` (D42): the two codes never appear together, and neither appears when there is no interval at all, which `no_interval` covers. (3) The p-value: when `headline.skill` is null, `p_value` and `n_permutations` are null and `p_value_reason` says why. (4) The leak screen, spec step 8: a column whose single-column skill cannot be computed is not flagged and gets no warning. The application already behaves so; keep it. (5) `stages.skill("mse", score, 0)` returns None (spec 2.7). (6) The command line finishes on such a table: the summary must not fail on a null skill. Schema: spec 5.2. The gate's dataset is `flat_tail`, daily sales that stop: the target is 0 from 65% of the way through the series to its end, so the previous value predicts every holdout row exactly.

tasks.title: Colliding feature names stop the run
tasks.why_tier: A clear contract in spec step 5: one check, one named error. It decides no number.
tasks.brief: The preprocessed matrix names a numeric feature by its own name and each level of a categorical feature `<column>=<level>`. Today, when two of those names are the same, one column silently overwrites the other: a numeric column named `colour=red` beside a categorical `colour` with the level `red` reaches no model and is still listed as a feature (D37). Add the named error `FeatureNameCollisionError`, code `feature_name_collision`, to `mlprofessor/errors.py`, and raise it from `profile()` as spec step 5 says ('Feature names must be distinct'): after the column roles, before the row cap, the split, the leak screen and any fit, with nothing written. The message names every column involved. Which names are compared is pinned there and is the point of this task: the columns that are features after step 5; for a categorical column EVERY level among the usable rows, not only the 30 a fit keeps, with `(missing)` when a usable row has a missing cell, a level being the cell's text without the white space round it (D42), as the application already has it; decided before the row cap, so that `fast` and `full` agree and no seed changes the outcome. A level that sits only in rows with no target does not count. Two categorical columns can collide too (`site` with the level `a=b`, beside `site=a` with the level `b`). `stages.Preprocessor.fit` raises the same error when two of the names it would give are the same, judged on the levels it keeps from the rows it is given (spec 2.7). The command line exits 3 with `error: feature_name_collision: ...`, as for any named error.

tasks.title: A configuration that fails after it is chosen
tasks.why_tier: Decides which configuration the headline comes from, and must not let the holdout take part in the choice.
tasks.brief: Spec steps 9 to 11 (D38). The application already falls back to the next best configuration by `cv_mean` when the chosen one raises on the final fit or while predicting the holdout, and already raises `all_models_failed` when none is left: keep both. What is wrong today is that the failed configuration's record is wiped: its fold scores, `cv_mean` and `cv_std` are set to null, so the models table misreports what was tried. Change that: a configuration that fails AFTER it was chosen gets status `failed`, its error text and a `model_failed` warning, and KEEPS the `fold_scores`, `cv_mean` and `cv_std` it had. A configuration that fails DURING selection is unchanged: all five fold scores null, `cv_mean` and `cv_std` null (a first-pass test pins that). The headline comes from exactly one configuration, the first in the ranking of step 9 whose refit and holdout prediction both succeed; `headline`, `cv.chosen`, `cv.chosen_mean`, the predictions, the interval and the p-value are its alone. Holdout rows are handed to one configuration at a time, in ranking order, and to none once one has predicted them. The holdout plays no part in the choice: a configuration is passed over only for raising, never for its score.

tasks.title: Small defects: the output folder, process settings, the no-features message, the console summary
tasks.why_tier: Four small contracts, each stated in spec 2.1, 2.2 or 2.4.
tasks.brief: Four defects from the first review (D39). (1) An `out_dir` that cannot be used is an `InputError` raised before anything is loaded (spec 2.1): the path, or the nearest folder above it that exists, is something other than a folder, for one when it names an existing file. Today that is an unnamed FileExistsError after the whole run. Check it with the other arguments, without creating anything. (2) Process-wide settings are left as the caller had them, whether `profile()` or a function of `stages` returns or raises (spec 2.1). The one found: the loader raises `csv.field_size_limit` for the whole process and never puts it back. Restore the caller's value in a `finally`. (3) The message of `no_features` names every excluded column and, for each, its reason as `columns[].reason` spells it (spec 2.4), both when no column is a feature after step 5 and when the leak screen removes the last one. Today it says 'see the column accounting', and an error returns none. (4) The console summary (spec 2.2) also shows: the interval on the score and the interval on skill, each end as a number, or the text of `headline.interval_reason` when there is no interval; the p-value as a number, or the text of `headline.p_value_reason` when there is none; and one line per warning holding its code and, when it has one, its column. A number counts as shown when it is printed to within 0.0005 x max(1, |value|) of the value in `profile.json`. The wording stays yours; keep it short and plain. A null skill, or a null interval on skill, needs no number: the line of its `skill_undefined` or `no_skill_interval` warning covers it.

tasks.why_tier: Prose and three command lines, from known facts.

tasks.title: Guard of the third pass: a line pandas reads as the header. No code change expected
tasks.why_tier: Nothing is built here. But if the guard fails, the fix is in the loader's own reading of the header line, where taking the wrong line for the header loses a column without a word.
tasks.brief: NO CODE CHANGE IS EXPECTED. `tests/test_guard_header_lines.py` guards behaviour the application already has: its one test was measured to pass against the application on 2026-11-20, in all three of its cases, before this task existed (plan/test-plan.md, 'Third pass'). Run it first. If it passes, change nothing and finish. If it fails, THE APPLICATION IS WRONG, NOT THE TEST: the test is locked, and it was proved by running it against a copy of the reference implementation whose check for long rows had been taken out (F6d, spec section 8), on which it fails. What it guards: a first line of a form feed, of a no-break space, or of two quotes round a space, before a header of two columns. pandas does not skip such a line. It reads it as a header of one column, and every line after it, the real header among them, then has more fields than the header. The loader must stop with `input_error` (spec section 6), from `stages.load_table` and from `profile()`, and write nothing. The trap: Python's `str.strip()` removes a form feed and a no-break space, and pandas skips only spaces and tabs, so a loader that picks the header line with the default `strip()` and then trusts pandas' column count reads one column and loses the other. Fix only what the failing test names, and say in your final message what you found. This test joins the checks every later task must keep green.

tasks.title: No number that is not finite is reported, or turned into null
tasks.why_tier: Decides whether a number may be reported at all, and which error the caller gets when it may not; it also changes which feature values reach a model.
tasks.brief: A regression target holding one sentinel-sized cell (1.7976931348623157e308 among values near 20), or a target on the scale of 1e160, finishes today with `score`, `baseline_score` and `skill` null, a p-value all the same, and no warning. The square of such a value is beyond the largest double, so the squared error is infinite, and `mlprofessor/result.py` turns every number that is not finite into null as the result is built (D44). Nothing may be written as null because it overflowed. Follow spec section 3, 'Numbers that are not finite', rule by rule. (1) Add the error `NonFiniteScoreError`, code `non_finite_score`, to `mlprofessor/errors.py`. (2) Score every baseline of step 11 on the holdout as soon as the split is made, before the leak screen and before any step or model is fitted. If a baseline's score is not finite, raise the new error there. Under time order with unique timestamps check both baselines. The order is the point: with a target too large for squared error the caller must get this one error, never `all_models_failed` with a list of configurations. (3) In the leak screen, for regression: if the pooled squared error of a baseline it uses (each fold's training mean; the previous value), or of the column's own tree, is not finite, raise the new error. Today a skill that is not-a-number is read as 'not flagged'. (4) During selection a configuration whose prediction is not finite is already failed: keep that. Treat a fold score that is not finite in the same way: status `failed`, an error text, a `model_failed` warning, five null fold scores, never chosen. Today such a configuration keeps the status `fitted` with a null `cv_mean`, and can still be chosen. (5) After the choice, a prediction for the holdout that is not finite already counts as raising, with the fallback of D38: keep that. If the predictions are finite and the holdout score is not, raise the new error and do NOT try the next configuration: a configuration is passed over only for raising, never for its score. (6) If the headline skill comes out not finite from a finite score and a finite baseline score, raise the new error. Skill is null only for a baseline score of exactly zero. (7) Before the result is returned or written, check that every number of `validation`, `headline`, `baselines`, `cv` and `models` is finite, and raise the new error if one is not. The conversion in `result.py` must not be what stands between a not-a-number and the output. (8) A p-value is reported only when skill is a number; with (6) and (7) that follows. (9) The message of the new error names the number: a baseline by its name as `baselines[].name` spells it (`training_mean`, `previous_value`), a configuration by its name as `models[].config` spells it, a field of the output by its key. It also gives the likely cause, such as a target value too large for squared error. (10) Three quiet fallbacks the review found, and a fourth of the same kind. None may stay as a silent default. `pipeline.py` reads a regression target with `errors="coerce"`: the target is of integer or float type there (step 4) and nothing can be coerced, so convert it plainly. `leakage.py` drops the previous-value baseline when a previous value is missing: none ever is (spec step 8, 'The previous value exists for every row it is asked for'); if one is, raise an internal error, do not fall back to the training mean. `preprocess.py` reads a deviation that is not finite as 1: with part (11) no such deviation can arise, so remove the special case and keep only 'a zero deviation is read as 1'. `pipeline.py` passes over a panel autocorrelation that is not finite: when the per-timestamp means do not vary there is no value and no warning, as now; when the number overflows, raise the new error. (11) D48: a numeric feature cell whose magnitude is above 3.4028234663852886e+38, the largest 32-bit float, is read exactly as an infinite cell is: missing, counted in `n_infinite`, named by the column's `infinite_values` warning, NaN to a step supplied through the seam, imputed in the matrix. scikit-learn's trees read 32-bit floats, and today one such cell stops the run with a raw `ValueError` from the leak screen. Apply the rule wherever a feature value is read: `stages.column_roles`, the leak screen, the feature frame, and `stages.Preprocessor` itself, in `fit` and in `transform`. A value of exactly that magnitude is kept. A target value of that size is not missing. (12) D48: a complex-number target is not numeric. `task="regression"` on it is `task_unsupported`; under `task="auto"` two distinct values are classification and anything else is `task_ambiguous`. Today it runs as a regression and loses its imaginary part. tasks.title: Copies of a holdout row among the training rows stop the run; the `duplicates` argument
tasks.why_tier: Decides whether a headline may be reported at all, and on which evidence: which rows count as copies of which.
tasks.brief: D49, D53, D54. On pure noise with every row present twice the full profile reports skill 0.918 with p = 0.001: a quarter of the rows go to the holdout at random, so three quarters of the holdout rows have their copy among the training rows, and a model that can recall a row scores on them. Build spec step 8a. (1) A tenth parameter of `profile()`, `duplicates`, after `n_jobs`, with the default `"error"`; the other value is `"keep"`. Anything else, a value that is not text among them (`True`, `None`, `1`), is an `InputError` raised with the other argument checks, before anything is loaded. `--duplicates error|keep` on the command line, declared with its two choices as `--task` and `--profile` are, so that any other value is refused when the command line is parsed (exit 2), and shown by `profile --help`. tasks.title: Whole numbers are compared exactly: integer time keys, distinct values, and whole numbers too large for 64 bits
tasks.why_tier: Decides which rows share a timestamp, and so the holdout, the folds and whether the previous-value baseline exists; and decides whether a column reaches a model.
tasks.brief: D50, D53. Three faults with one cause: whole numbers are turned into 64-bit floats, which hold every whole number only up to 2**53. (1) Integer time keys (spec step 3, 2.7). `mlprofessor/split.py` reads a numeric time column as float64, so 600 distinct nanosecond instants 100 nanoseconds apart become 235 timestamps: `timestamps_unique` is false, the previous-value baseline is gone, and a random walk is scored against the training mean. For an integer-typed column (any width, signed or unsigned, nullable or not, sparse or not) that holds at least one value of magnitude ABOVE 2**53, judged over its non-missing loaded values, the keys are the 64-bit integers themselves: `int64`, or `uint64` for an unsigned type. They are compared as integers everywhere a key is used: the order of the rows, the fast profile's cap, the count of distinct timestamps, which rows share a timestamp, the split, the gap, the previous value, the blocks of the bootstrap. `validation.train_end`, `holdout_start` and `holdout_end` are then written as those integers, exactly. `stages.read_time` returns such keys with that integer type, each equal to its value, and `stages.split_time` and `stages.previous_value` take them without turning them into floats. Up to a magnitude of 2**53 nothing changes: the keys stay float64, which a locked test of `read_time` requires. A float column is ordered as the floats it holds. (2) Distinct values (spec step 5, rules 8, 8a, 8b). `mlprofessor/columns.py` counts the distinct values of a numeric column on float64, so an unsigned column holding 50 distinct values near 2**63 is reported `constant`. For an integer-typed column judge all three rules on the integers themselves: the number of distinct values, whether every value is distinct, whether they are strictly increasing or decreasing down the file, and whether the largest minus the smallest plus one equals their count. Work that last one out in Python integers, or compare neighbours: `numpy.diff` on the two ends of the int64 range overflows without a word. The values handed to a step and to the models stay float64 (spec 2.6). (3) Whole numbers too large for 64 bits (spec step 1a, last points; 2.4; section 6). pandas loads a CSV column holding a whole number beyond 64 bits as an `object` column of Python integers, and a DataFrame can hold one; `mlprofessor/load.py` calls `numpy.isinf` on such a value and a raw `TypeError` reaches the caller in every role. An object column whose non-missing values are all whole numbers and do not all fit in 64 bits (neither all within -2**63 to 2**63 - 1 nor all within 0 to 2**64 - 1) is: as a spare column, excluded with the reason `unsupported_type` and one warning of the code `unsupported_type` naming the column; as the target, `task_unsupported` whatever task was asked for; as the time column, `time_column_invalid`. Never a raw exception, from a CSV or from a DataFrame, through `profile()` or the command line (exit 3, one line). An object column of whole numbers that DO fit is the next task's; leave it as it is here. The gate check `time.integer_keys_distinct` is yours: a random walk of 1,500 rows whose time column is int64 nanoseconds, 100 apart from 1.7e18. tasks.title: Number columns as a database driver returns them; a warning for every unsupported column

tasks.brief: D51. A database driver returns a column of numbers as Python objects: `decimal.Decimal`, `True`/`False` with `None`, whole numbers with `None`. pandas types such a column `object`, and today it is excluded as `unsupported_type` with nothing said; on the third review's table the skill was -0.011, against 0.779 with the same values in typed columns. Build spec step 1a. Before any other step, look once at each `object` column, over all its loaded rows, and read it by what its non-missing cells are: all booleans (`bool`, `numpy.bool_`): a boolean column. All whole numbers held exactly, and all fitting in 64 bits: a whole-number column, every value exact (signed when all are within -2**63 to 2**63 - 1, unsigned when all are within 0 to 2**64 - 1). A whole number held exactly is a Python or numpy integer, or a `Decimal` with no fractional part (`Decimal("7")`, `Decimal("1E+3")`): a driver returns a wide whole-number column that way, and D50 forbids merging its values. All whole numbers, not all fitting: too large for 64 bits, which the task before this one built. Numbers of any mixture (whole numbers, `float`, `numpy.floating`, any `Decimal`) with at least one that is not a whole number held exactly: a column of 64-bit floats, each value through `float()`; a value beyond the largest double becomes infinite with its sign (`float()` of a huge Python integer raises `OverflowError`: catch it). Anything else is left as it is and stays `unsupported_type`: a boolean beside a number (`True` and `3`) is not guessed, nor is text beside a number, nor a complex number. An empty cell stays empty: `None`, NaN, `pd.NA`, `NaT`, and a `Decimal` not-a-number of either kind. pandas itself raises `decimal.InvalidOperation` on `Decimal("sNaN")`, from `isna()`, so find the empty cells of such a column yourself before pandas is asked. A `Decimal` infinity becomes an infinite float and is then what an infinite float is in that role. After this the column is THE SAME as a typed column holding those values, in every role and every step: a feature (numeric), the target (so a `Decimal` target is a regression target and `True`/`False` with `None` are two classes), the time column (so whole numbers held as objects are exact keys above 2**53, as the task before built for typed columns, and their distinct values are counted exactly), `stages.usable_rows`, `stages.column_roles`, `stages.decide_task`, `stages.read_time`, and what a seam-supplied step receives (floats). A table read straight from a database gives the result its typed twin gives, number for number. Two things are reported as loaded: `columns[].dtype` and `task.target_dtype` still say `object`. The target's values are written as read: `y_true`, `task.classes` and `task.positive_class` hold numbers or booleans. Then the warning (spec 2.5): every column still excluded with the reason `unsupported_type`, of any type (durations, periods, intervals, complex numbers, bytes, containers, mixed objects), gets exactly one warning of the code `unsupported_type` naming it, so that it shows in the console summary. Do the conversion in one place and have every role read the converted column, rather than teaching each rule about objects.

tasks.title: One to nine digits in a fraction of a second; a refusal that says what is wrong
tasks.why_tier: A clear contract in spec step 3: which text is accepted as a time value, and what a refusal says. The order of the rows follows from pandas' own parsing.
tasks.brief: D52. `mlprofessor/split.py` accepts an ISO 8601 time value with exactly three digits in its fraction of a second, so a CSV that pandas itself wrote from microsecond timestamps (six digits) stops with `time_column_invalid`, and the message says the value 'is not ISO 8601 with the year first', which is false. What each holds: (M20; the fourth review, finding 3) `columns[].n_infinite` of a numeric target and of a numeric time column counts their infinite cells, each of which is a missing target or a missing time value; `n_missing` does not count them and no `infinite_values` warning is raised for those two columns (spec steps 2 and 5, 5.2). The reference implementation left them out until this pass, and the guard fails on a copy of it that still does (M20, spec 8.1). (D57, ruled) In an object target that is not read as numbers (text classes beside a few floats), a cell holding an infinite float, Python's or numpy's, is a missing target: its row is dropped and counted in `dropped_missing_target`, and the cell in the target's `n_infinite`; a target of one text value and infinite floats alone is `target_constant` (spec step 2). An object target in which every value is a number is floats by step 1a, and an infinite one there is a missing target as in any numeric column. (Ruled) `mlprofessor.ProfileResult(document, predictions)` is the pinned constructor: a result made from the `to_dict()` and the `predictions` of another equals it in every member (spec 2.3). (Spec 2.6) A regression model whose `predict` returns a column of n values for n rows is read as n values and stays `fitted`; one that returns another number of values is `failed`. Fix only what a failing test names, and say in your final message which tests failed before your change.

tasks.title: Each object column is read once, over all loaded rows (the fourth review, finding 1)
tasks.why_tier: Decides whether a run may go ahead: a cell in a row that is dropped for another column's empty cell either stops the run with a named error or is silently left out of the reading of its column.
tasks.brief: D57; spec step 1a ('Each column is read once'), step 3. Step 1a reads an object column that holds only numbers as the typed column it stands for. The application applies that reading to the usable rows only, so a cell that decides what the column is goes unseen when its row is dropped for another column's empty cell, and the run goes ahead on a column it would have refused. The fourth review lists five tables, and on all five the application returns a result today. Build: the reading of step 1a is made ONCE for each object column, over ALL of its loaded rows, before step 2, and every later step goes by it. The five tables, each a test of `tests/test_read_once.py`: (1) an object target of whole numbers with one text cell in a row that has no time value: the same named error as when that cell is in a usable row (`task_ambiguous` under task='auto', the column being text beside numbers); (2) an object target of whole numbers with one whole number too large for 64 bits in a row with no time value: `task_unsupported`; (3) an object time column of whole numbers with one text cell in a row with no target: `time_column_invalid`, as in a usable row; (4) a time column of Python integers with one too large for 64 bits in a row with no target: `time_column_invalid`; (5) an int64 time column whose one value above 2**53 is in a row with no target: the run finishes, and because step 3 judges 'at least one value above 2**53' over the non-missing LOADED values, the keys are exact integers and `validation.train_end`, `holdout_start` and `holdout_end` are written as whole numbers (17900 and 18000 on the test's table, not 17900.0). An empty cell stays empty and decides nothing, as before. `stages` reads a column as `profile()` does (spec 2.7). Nothing else changes: a table with no such cell gives the output it gave before, value for value.

tasks.title: No part of the output can hold a number that is not finite; the boundary of a failed configuration; the three-class message (the fourth review, findings 4 and 5)
tasks.why_tier: Decides whether a result may exist at all, and what counts as a model's failure against a fault of the tool's own scoring.
tasks.brief: D57; spec 2.3, 'Numbers that are not finite' rule 6, steps 4, 9, 10 and 13. Three things. (1) FINDING 4. The check that no number of the output is infinite or not-a-number covers five parts of the document today (`validation`, `headline`, `baselines`, `cv`, `models`); a float that is not finite in any other part is turned into null when the result is made. Make it cover EVERY part: `meta`, `input`, `rows`, `columns`, `task` and `warnings` as well, lists and nested records included, for Python floats and numpy floats alike. The check is made in the constructor, `ProfileResult(document, predictions)`, which is pinned: constructing a result from a document that holds such a float anywhere raises `NonFiniteScoreError` (`non_finite_score`), and the message names the number by its key. A result made from the `to_dict()` of another still equals it. `tests/test_review4_small.py` plants one such float in each of eight parts. (2) FINDING 5, WHICH HAS NO TEST: read spec step 9, 'What can fail a configuration, and what cannot'. A configuration is recorded as failed for what the model does and for nothing else: making the estimator, its `fit`, its prediction, and the reading of what it handed back (the shape of spec 2.6 and the check that every value is finite); and a fold score that is not finite fails it too. The tool's own scoring of a fold is NOT inside that `try`: if scoring finite predictions of the right shape raises, that is a defect of the tool and the exception must end the run, not be written into the models table as `failed`. Check the selection loop and the fit after selection (step 10) against that paragraph and narrow any `except` that covers the tool's own arithmetic. No input reaches the scoring with predictions that are not already one finite number for each row, which is why no test can show this; it is judged by reading. Say in your final message what the `try` covered before and what it covers now. (3) THE THREE-CLASS MESSAGE. Under task='auto', a target that is not numeric with three or more distinct values raises `task_ambiguous` as now, with a message that says three or more classes are not supported (in those words), gives the number of distinct values, says what would run (the rows of two classes, or the classes merged into two), and does NOT suggest declaring the task: it holds neither `task=` nor the word `declare`, since no declared task would run. For a numeric target with 3 to 20 distinct values the message says the same of three or more classes and adds that a quantity can be run with `task='regression'`, in those words (spec step 4).

tasks.brief: D58 part 1; spec 2.1 (`time_col`), 2.2, 2.4 (`time_order_undeclared`), 2.5 (`date_column_undeclared`), step 5, step 8a, 5.2 (`input.time_col`). On real data the VIX level with its date column undeclared was reported at skill 0.939, against 0.023 with it declared. Build: (1) `time_col` takes a column's name, `None`, or `False`. `False` is the caller's statement that the order of the rows in time does not matter; `True` is an `InputError`; `gap` above 0 with `time_col=False` is an `InputError`, as with `None`. (2) A new error, `TimeOrderUndeclaredError`, code `time_order_undeclared`. When `time_col` is `None` and at least one column would be excluded with the reason `datetime` (rule 2 or rule 4 of step 5), the run stops with it at step 5: before the row cap, the split, the leak screen and any fit, and nothing is written. Its message holds the name of every such column, each in quotes as `repr` writes it, and the texts `time_col`, `--time-col`, `time_col=False` and `--no-time-order`. Because step 5 comes before step 8a, such a table stops with this error and never with `holdout_copies_in_training`. (3) With `time_col=False` the run goes ahead under the random scheme exactly as it does today with `None`: the column is excluded as `datetime`, one `date_column_undeclared` warning names it, `validation.caveat` is the random caveat, `validation.time_col` is null, and `input.time_col` is `false` (it records the argument as passed: a name, false or null). The copies error of step 8a can then follow, and its message names the date column as it does today. On a table with no date column `time_col=False` changes nothing but `input.time_col`. With a time column declared, another date column is excluded with no stop and no warning, as today. (4) The command line: `--no-time-order`, taking no value, is `time_col=False`; it cannot be given with `--time-col` (argparse refuses the pair, exit 2, nothing written); `profile --help` shows it. (5) `stages.column_roles` does not raise the new error: `profile()` does. (6) THE README, IN THIS SAME TASK. `examples/customers.csv` has a column of dates, `signup_date`, so once the stop is built every README command that profiles it with no time column stops. Customers are not ordered in time: add `--no-time-order` to each such command, and `time_col=False` to the Python example, with one sentence saying why. `tests/test_readme_examples.py::test_every_readme_command_runs` runs every command in the README: it is green before this task and MUST BE GREEN AFTER IT, so change the application and the commands together and run that test before you finish. The fuller account of the new arguments is T47's. The gate: two of its runs now pass `--no-time-order` (`messy`, and `time_blocks` with no time column), so the four checks that read them fail on the application until this task and are owned by it, with the new `time.undeclared_stops`. Several older tests were loosened to accept the stop (plan/test-plan.md, 'Fifth pass', rule 3): they pass before and after.

tasks.title: A declared entity column under the random scheme: `group_col`, the grouped split, the cap, the interval
tasks.why_tier: Decides which rows are training rows and which are holdout rows, and how the interval on the headline is computed.
tasks.brief: D57 part 1; spec 2.1 (`group_col`), 2.2, 2.4, 2.7, steps 2, 5, 6, 7, 8a, 12, 4.2, 5.2, 5.4, section 7. When one customer, patient or device has several rows, a random split of rows puts the same entity on both sides and a model scores by knowing it again: on the gate's `entities` table the right skill is zero and a row-by-row split gives 0.76 to 0.88. Build: (1) An eleventh parameter of `profile()`, `group_col`, after `duplicates`, default `None`: a column's name, `None`, or `False` (the caller's statement that there are no entities: it is recorded and, in this task, changes nothing else). Any other value that is not text, `group_col` equal to `target` or to `time_col`: `InputError`, before anything is loaded. A name that is not a column: `column_not_found`. `--group-col COLUMN` and `--no-entities` on the command line, mutually exclusive (exit 2 for both together). `input.group_col` records the argument as passed. (2) The column gets the role `group` in `columns`, with `kind` and `reason` null; it is never a feature and no rule of step 5 is applied to it. How it is read is spec step 5, 'How an entity column is read': equal cells are one entity, text without the white space round it, whole numbers exactly at any size, 0.0 and -0.0 one value. An entity cell that is empty, or text of only white space, in a usable row: `group_column_invalid` (new error class `GroupColumnError`), naming the column; in a row dropped for its target it is of no account. Values that cannot be compared for equality (lists, dictionaries, sets): `group_column_invalid`. (3) THE SPLIT, with no time column: the grouped scheme of spec step 7. Read its five numbered properties; they are the contract, the row numbers are not. No entity has rows on both sides of the holdout; within the training rows every entity is in the validation part of exactly one fold, whole; the holdout is whole entities taken in an order drawn from the seed until they hold at least a quarter of the rows, and for classification that is done for the entities of each class apart (an entity counts with the class most of its rows hold, the positive class on a tie); the folds are dealt as evenly as whole entities allow; and the split depends on which rows share an entity and not on what the entities are called. Fewer than six entities, or fewer than five left for the folds: `too_few_groups` (new error class `TooFewGroupsError`). `stages.split_random` gains `groups=None` and must be the code `profile()` uses (spec 2.7): a test compares the two. `validation.scheme` is `grouped`, `validation.caveat` the fixed text of the grouped scheme (spec 5.4), `validation.group_col` the column, `n_groups_training` and `n_groups_holdout` the entities on each side, `stratified` true for classification. Without an entity column those keys are null and nothing else changes. Every row its own entity is allowed. (4) THE FAST PROFILE'S CAP with an entity column (step 6): whole entities, taken in an order drawn from the seed, each kept when all of its rows still fit under 2,000; so every entity is kept whole or left out whole, and none left out would have fitted. When the cap leaves too few entities and every usable row together could be split: `fast_profile_too_few_rows`; when the full profile would stop too, its own error. (5) THE RULE ON COPIES (step 8a) applies under the grouped scheme as under the random one: the count and the share are reported, and copies across entities stop the run unless `duplicates='keep'`. (6) THE INTERVAL AND THE P-VALUE (step 12): under the grouped scheme each resample draws whole entities of the holdout, as many as it has, with replacement, and takes every row of each; method `bootstrap_groups`. With fewer than 30 entities in the holdout there is no interval, with a reason and the `no_interval` warning. There is no p-value under the grouped scheme: `p_value` and `n_permutations` are null and `p_value_reason` says that shuffling assumes independent rows (it holds the words `independent rows`). The rows of one entity are not independent: measured on `entities`, an interval from single rows left the true value outside in 11 of 30 runs and a row shuffle gave p below 0.05 in 5 of 30 (spec 10.7). Under time order `group_col` is accepted and recorded and its role is `group`; what it changes there is T44's.

tasks.title: Entities under time order: each entity's own previous value, the leak screen's baseline, and the stop for a panel with no entity declared
tasks.why_tier: Decides the baseline the headline is measured against, the baseline the leak screen excludes columns by, and whether a panel may be profiled at all without the caller's word.
tasks.brief: D57 part 1 and D58 part 3; spec 2.4 (`entities_undeclared`, `group_column_invalid`), 2.5 (`no_previous_value`, `autocorrelated_panel_target`), 2.7 (`previous_value`), steps 7, 8, 11, 12, 5.2. On real data a panel of five stock prices scored against the training mean was reported at skill 0.979. Build, for a regression under time order: (1) WITH AN ENTITY COLUMN the split is by time exactly as before (an entity is on both sides: earlier rows in training, later ones in the holdout), and the second baseline, `previous_value`, is each entity's own: for a row, the target of the latest row of the same entity that lies at least `gap + 1` distinct timestamps earlier, the timestamps being those of all the time-ordered usable rows after the row cap, whatever their entity, and rows inside the gap counting as earlier rows. So an entity's first holdout row is predicted from its last training row. A holdout row whose entity has no such earlier row has no previous value: for it the baseline predicts the training mean; `validation.n_holdout_without_previous` counts those rows, and when it is above zero one `no_previous_value` warning (column null) says so. Both baselines are scored and reported and the headline baseline is the one with the lower squared error, a tie going to `training_mean`, as with unique timestamps. Two rows of one entity at one timestamp, among the rows split: `group_column_invalid`, with the number of such rows (in a classification nothing asks this, and such a table runs). `stages.previous_value` gains `groups=None` (spec 2.7). `validation.group_col`, `n_groups_training` and `n_groups_holdout` are reported under time order too: the entities that have a training row, and those that have a holdout row. The interval is the block bootstrap as before. (2) THE LEAK SCREEN (step 8) measures a column against the lower of each fold's training mean and the previous value, and with an entity column that previous value is each entity's own; a validation row whose entity has none is given its fold's training mean in its place. Without this the lag of a persistent panel is excluded as a leak for being as good as the baseline it must beat. (3) WITH REPEATED TIMESTAMPS AND NO ENTITY COLUMN, where today the `autocorrelated_panel_target` warning is raised (the lag-1 autocorrelation of the per-timestamp mean of the target over the training timestamps is above 0.5): when `group_col` is `None` the run STOPS with a new error, `EntitiesUndeclaredError`, code `entities_undeclared`, as soon as the split is made, before the leak screen and any fit; nothing is written. Its message holds the texts `group_col`, `--group-col`, `group_col=False` and `--no-entities`. When the caller passed `group_col=False` the run goes ahead exactly as it does today, with the baseline `training_mean` and the warning. At or below 0.5, and where the means do not vary, nothing changes. Two older tests were loosened to accept the stop (plan/test-plan.md, 'Fifth pass', rule 3).

tasks.title: `duplicates="group"`: each set of copies on one side of the split and of every fold
tasks.why_tier: Decides which rows are training rows and which are holdout rows, and whether a table with copies may be profiled.
tasks.brief: D57 part 3, as amended by D60; spec 2.1 (`duplicates`), 2.2, 2.5 (`copies_grouped`), steps 7 and 8a, 5.2 (`n_rows_with_copies`). The broader screen for repeated rows is NOT part of this version (D60): a copy is still an exact copy, as step 8a defines it, and D49's rule, its cut-off and its error are unchanged. Do not build any wider notion of a repeat. Build the third value of `duplicates`: (1) `"group"` is accepted by `profile()` and by `--duplicates` (three choices now; anything else is refused as before). (2) With `duplicates="group"` and no time column, BEFORE the split, on the feature columns of step 5 (the leak screen has not run yet) and over all the rows that are split (after the row cap, which is the ordinary random sample when no entity column is declared): find the sets of rows that are copies of one another, the same value in every such column and the same target, compared as step 8a compares them. `validation.n_rows_with_copies` is the number of rows that have a copy among them (0 when none has; null with any other value of `duplicates` and under time order). When it is above zero, each set is a unit of the grouped split of T43: no set has rows on both sides of the holdout or in two folds; `validation.scheme` is `grouped`; `n_groups_training` and `n_groups_holdout` count the units (a row with no copy is a unit of its own); the interval is `bootstrap_groups` over the units and there is no p-value; and one `copies_grouped` warning (column null) says so. When no row has a copy the split is the random scheme's, row for row, the scheme is `random`, and nothing is said. (3) WITH AN ENTITY COLUMN AS WELL the two are joined: two rows are in one unit when they are of one entity or copies of one another, directly or through other rows, so a set of copies that spans two entities joins them. (4) STEP 8A is still run and reported: after the split `n_holdout_copies` is normally 0. One case is left: when the leak screen excludes a column, rows that differed only in it become copies and may be on opposite sides; they are counted, and when the rule is met the run stops with `holdout_copies_in_training`, whose message then holds the word `group` and the name of every column excluded as a suspected leak. Below the rule the run goes ahead. (5) The message of `holdout_copies_in_training` under the default now names three ways on: it holds the words `group` and `keep` (and everything it held before). Under time order `duplicates="group"` changes nothing, like `"keep"`. `input.duplicates` records the value.

tasks.title: The type matrix gains a role: every kind of column as the entity column
tasks.why_tier: No input may end in an error that is not named (D52): this is the proof of it for the new role, across every type of column.
tasks.brief: D52, D57; spec section 7, 'The type matrix', 'The entity role', and step 5, 'How an entity column is read'. `tests/test_type_matrix_group.py` runs `profile()` with every kind of pandas column as `group_col`: every kind and every extreme of the first matrix with a 0/1 target and no time column, and every kind with its ordinary values under a numeric time column with a numeric target; 353 cases. Each must end in a result (which reports the column with the role `group`, keeps the reconciliation rules and is strict JSON) or in a named error, a subclass of `ProfileError`; never in a `TypeError`, a `ValueError`, an `OverflowError` or any other raw exception. Run the file; for each failing case find where the exception starts and make the entity column's reading handle that kind there: sparse columns, nullable types, categories, bytes, dates in any unit and zone, durations, periods, intervals, complex numbers, `Decimal` values (a signalling not-a-number among them: pandas raises on it, so it must not be handed to pandas), whole numbers beyond 64 bits (a fine entity column: compared exactly), tuples, and the containers that cannot be compared (lists, dictionaries, sets: `group_column_invalid`). An all-missing entity column is `group_column_invalid` by the rule for an empty cell. NEVER a broad `except` round the run: the remedy is at the place the exception starts. Which of the two ends a case has is not what this file pins; `tests/test_groups_random.py` and `tests/test_groups_time.py` pin the rules.

tasks.brief: D56 to D60. Bring the README up to date with this pass, in plain words and in your own wording. (1) The entity column: `group_col` in the Python example and `--group-col` on the command line; what an entity is (a customer, a patient, a device, one series of a panel); that with no time column its rows stay on one side of the split and of every fold (the scheme is `grouped`, the interval comes from whole entities and there is no p-value), and that under time order each entity has its own previous value as a baseline. Say why in a sentence each: a headline the tool has reason to think inflated is printed only when the caller has said the reason does not apply. (3) `duplicates='group'` beside `error` and `keep`: each set of exact copies is kept on one side of the split. (4) THE LIMIT, STATED PLAINLY: a copy of a row is detected only when it agrees in every feature column and the target; a copy that differs in any column (an added column, a batch number, a small change to a value) is not detected in this version, and when the caller knows which rows belong together `group_col` is the control. Do not soften this sentence and do not promise a date. (5) The smaller changes: the infinite cells of the target and of the time column are counted in their column records; an object column is read once, over all its rows; three or more classes are not supported. Every command shown must still work as written (`tests/test_readme_examples.py` runs them), and the README names no file under `verify/` or `tests/`.
